policy_name: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (White Paper, CP 815) and Government response (CP 1019)
issuing_authority: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT); presented to Parliament by the Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology
regulatory_regime: Non-statutory, principles-based framework implemented by existing sectoral regulators (e.g. ICO, CMA, FCA, Ofcom, MHRA, EHRC) within existing powers
geo_constraints: United Kingdom; applied by UK regulators within their existing remits

locale_context.regulation: Soft law · non-statutory principles applied by existing sector regulators
locale_context.culture: UK common-law, pro-innovation, regulator-led culture: context-specific, sectoral guidance rather than new horizontal legislation.

key_dates.event: Policy paper 'Establishing a pro-innovation approach to regulating AI' published
White Paper (CP 815) presented to Parliament; consultation opened
Government response (CP 1019) published, confirming non-statutory, regulator-led approach; key regulators asked to publish their strategic approaches to AI by April 2024
New government's King's Speech signals intent to legislate for the most powerful AI models; no bill subsequently introduced
AI Opportunities Action Plan published (policy emphasis shifts to growth/adoption)
King's Speech contains no standalone AI bill; a 'Regulating for Growth Bill' (incl. AI Growth Lab sandbox powers) announced — parliamentary stage unverified

version: CP 815 (29 March 2023), with correction slip; Government response CP 1019 (6 February 2024)
covered_entities: AI life cycle actors (developers, deployers, users) via regulator guidance
covered_systems: AI systems defined by reference to 'adaptivity' and 'autonomy'
highly capable general-purpose AI (addressed further in the 2024 government response)
exceptions: The non-statutory approach creates no new rights or routes to redress
Possible exemptions for regulators in areas such as national security to be considered before any statutory duty; defence governed by MoD AI principles
conditions: Principles applied by regulators proportionately, within existing remits and in accordance with existing law
Statutory duty on regulators anticipated only if monitoring shows non-statutory implementation is ineffective
objective: Establish a proportionate, context-specific and pro-innovation framework in which existing regulators apply five cross-sectoral principles to AI within their remits, supported by central government functions, rather than creating a new AI-specific regulator or horizontal AI law.
conflict_rule: Principles are applied 'in accordance with existing laws and regulations' (para. 50) and complement existing regulation; existing statutory duties (data protection, equality, consumer, sectoral law) prevail. 'conflicts_with' for the EU AI Act denotes a divergent regulatory philosophy (sectoral non-statutory vs horizontal statute), not a legal conflict.

sources_consulted: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-regulation-a-pro-innovation-approach (HTML text obtained via the Hugging Face dataset AndreasThinks/ukgov-policy-docs, a scrape of gov.uk policy papers)
record_provenance.notes: gov.uk could not be fetched directly in this session; clause text is taken from a third-party scrape of the gov.uk HTML version of CP 815 and should be re-checked against gov.uk. The February 2024 government response (CP 1019) text was not obtained; facts about it come from search results. As of Nov 2026 the UK has no AI-specific statute: the 2024 King's Speech commitment to legislate on the most powerful models has not resulted in a bill, and the May 2026 King's Speech (per law-firm and IAPP summaries) contained no standalone AI bill but announced a 'Regulating for Growth Bill' with AI Growth Lab sandbox powers — its introduction/stage could not be verified. The anticipated statutory 'due regard' duty on regulators has not been enacted. The white paper has not been formally withdrawn, but its status under the post-July-2024 government is best described as the existing non-statutory framework with policy emphasis shifted to the AI Opportunities Action Plan; 'voluntary' status reflects that it binds no one. Exact day of the July 2024 King's Speech (17 July) and the AI Opportunities Action Plan (13 January 2025) are from general knowledge.

clauses.original_text: 48. Existing regulators will be expected to implement the framework underpinned by 5 values-focused cross-sectoral principles: Safety, security and robustness Appropriate transparency and explainability Fairness Accountability and governance Contestability and redress
clauses.requirement: regulators implement the five principles within their remits
clauses.purpose: coherent, context-specific AI regulation without a new AI regulator
clauses.affected_asset: public trust; individuals affected by AI
clauses.applicable_systems: AI systems as characterized by adaptivity and autonomy
clauses.interpretation_notes: The five principles appear as a bulleted list in the source; line breaks collapsed here. 'Will be expected' is an expectation on regulators, not a legal duty (non-statutory).

clauses.section: Section 3.2.3, Principle: Safety, security, robustness — Definition and explanation
clauses.original_text: AI systems should function in a robust, secure and safe way throughout the AI life cycle, and risks should be continually identified, assessed and managed. Regulators may need to introduce measures for regulated entities to ensure that AI systems are technically secure and function reliably as intended throughout their entire life cycle.
clauses.action: ensure robust, secure and safe functioning; identify, assess and manage risks
clauses.requirement: AI systems function safely, securely and robustly with continual risk management
clauses.affected_asset: health, safety, critical infrastructure, system integrity
clauses.applicable_systems: any AI system within a regulator's remit
clauses.interpretation_notes: Principle text; any binding measures would come from regulators using existing powers.

clauses.section: Section 3.2.3, Principle: Fairness — Definition and explanation
clauses.original_text: AI systems should not undermine the legal rights of individuals or organisations, discriminate unfairly against individuals or create unfair market outcomes. Actors involved in all stages of the AI life cycle should consider definitions of fairness that are appropriate to a system’s use, outcomes and the application of relevant law.
clauses.action: not undermine rights / not discriminate unfairly; consider appropriate fairness definitions
clauses.requirement: avoid undermining legal rights, unfair discrimination and unfair market outcomes
clauses.affected_asset: legal rights of individuals and organisations; market competition
clauses.interpretation_notes: Rationale text links fairness to Equality Act 2010, Human Rights Act 1998, UK GDPR, consumer and competition law.

clauses.section: Section 3.2.3, Principle: Accountability and governance — Definition and explanation
clauses.original_text: Governance measures should be in place to ensure effective oversight of the supply and use of AI systems, with clear lines of accountability established across the AI life cycle.
clauses.actor: AI life cycle actors (organisations supplying or using AI)
clauses.action: put governance measures in place; establish clear lines of accountability
clauses.object: supply and use of AI systems
clauses.requirement: effective oversight and clear accountability across the AI life cycle
clauses.interpretation_notes: Regulators expected to place clear compliance expectations on appropriate supply-chain actors.

clauses.original_text: Where appropriate, users, impacted third parties and actors in the AI life cycle should be able to contest an AI decision or outcome that is harmful or creates material risk of harm. … The UK’s initial non-statutory approach will not create new rights or new routes to redress at this stage.
clauses.action: enable contestation of harmful AI decisions or outcomes
clauses.recipient: users, impacted third parties and AI life cycle actors
clauses.requirement: provide clear routes to contest harmful AI outcomes, using existing rights
clauses.condition: where appropriate; decision/outcome is harmful or creates material risk of harm
clauses.exception: no new rights or routes to redress are created by the non-statutory approach
clauses.interpretation_notes: Two non-adjacent sentences from the same principle joined with an ellipsis.

clauses.original_text: 57. Following a period of non-statutory implementation, and when parliamentary time allows, we anticipate that we will want to strengthen and clarify regulators’ mandates by introducing a new duty requiring them to have due regard to the principles.
clauses.object: duty on regulators to have due regard to the principles
clauses.requirement: possible future statutory 'due regard' duty on regulators
clauses.condition: after non-statutory implementation and when parliamentary time allows; dropped if monitoring shows it is unnecessary (para. 59)
clauses.interpretation_notes: Statement of intent, not an obligation; as of Nov 2026 no such duty has been legislated.
